This script contains analyses supporting the manuscript: “Prospect Theory and Judgments About Cognitive Enhancement” by Kianté Fernandez and John Medaglia

This script was prepared by Kianté Fernandez.

Last modified by Kianté Fernandez on 12/22/2020.

#Paper 1

Participants

A total of 616 participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk). MTurk allows researchers to collect high-quality data rapidly among demographically diverse individuals . Prior work has shown that MTurk can be reliably used to make inferences about a number of broader populations of interest . The participants were required to be located within the United States, over the age of 18, fluent in English. While limitations apply the MTurk studies (see Limitations in the Discussion), studies have shown that the quality of MTurk responses can improve with researcher constraints . In the current study, we required that participants had previously completed at least 100 tasks and maintained at least a 95% approval rating on MTurk. We additionally applied exclusions to further ensure that we analyzed high-quality behavioral data (see Exclusions). Our final sample was 425participants.The total sample consisted of 177 females, \(M_{age}\) = 36.36 years of age (\(SD_{age}\) = 11), with 114 high school, 242 undergraduate, and 68 postgraduate, and identified as White/Caucasian (n = 293), Asian (n = 44), Hispanic/Latino (n = 23), Black/African American (n = 41), Pacific Islander (n = 1) other/multiple (n = 13), or did not disclose their ethnicity (n = 2). The included subjects completed the task in an average of \(M_{task}\) = 7.79 minutes (\(SD_{task}\) = 10.04) and the survey in an average of \(M_{survey}\) = 19.27 minutes (\(SD_{survey}\) = 13.15).

Exlclusion Criteria

In line with recommendations for studies conducted using Amazons Mechanical Turk (AMT) service, careful instructions and exclusion criteria were applied to further ensure data quality . Using a multi-method approach to detect careless/invalid responses in online samples, several data exclusion criteria were applied . A total of 191 participants were excluded. Participants single trials were excluded if response times were either 250 milli-seconds or above 90 seconds. Given that participants had ample time to respond to each question (up to as long until they made a decision), we reasoned that these participants were not devoting sufficient attention to the task. Additionally, having considered trial wise exclusions, participants were also excluded for failure to complete at least 40 trials in the specified range. Finally, participants were excluded for failure of passing four attention check items and a total survey completion time below five minutes. Because our survey battery involved 11 different assessments, we reasoned that a total completion time below five minutes reflected a careless responder. Our overall exclusion rate of 31% is well in line with research findings studying quality control measures on MTurk .
